summary:
Guerrero stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition, and that framework is the only documented layer for this record. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that recognition is set state by state: 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative procedure, two more operated one in practice without enactment, six state legislatures had enacted nothing, and only seven states extended recognition to children.

Two higher authorities constrain what Guerrero may do. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors in the same year, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where a state has not enacted its own procedure, this national framework governs the visitor's expectations.

Human Rights Watch documents the practical consequence of an absent or obstructed procedure: identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

The Community Center for Inclusion's report of 6 March 2024 on Tabasco, a Mexican state with no legal gender-recognition procedure, records what that absence means at street level. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

The same report sets those barriers against lethal violence and impunity. A trans woman, Karina Gómez, was murdered in Villahermosa in August 2023, and more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.
tangentialFactors:
The Mexican picture is uneven rather than uniform. Two thirds of the states had legislated a recognition procedure by March 2025, two more administered one without legislation, and six had neither, so a trans visitor's document position depends heavily on which state the paper is issued in. Seven states extend recognition to children, which leaves most of the country without that provision.

Tabasco and Guanajuato serve as the documented examples of the wider pattern. The incidents Human Rights Watch records in those two states concern schools, clinics and employment, everyday settings rather than border or police settings, so document mismatch is the ordinary channel through which discrimination reaches a trans person.

The impunity figure is national and general rather than specific to trans victims: more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022. A trans person who is assaulted or killed can therefore expect little from the investigative process, and the Tabasco report places the murder of Karina Gómez in Villahermosa in August 2023 inside that context.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mexican states obtain recognition through the procedure their own legislature enacted, while Mexico's Supreme Court guidelines of 2022 bind all states and extend recognition to minors nationwide, giving residents a route even where local legislation is silent.

Where recognition is delayed or refused, residents carry documents that contradict their lived identity, which amplifies routine discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. The Tabasco findings show the resident-facing effect of a missing procedure: exclusion from employment, health services, education and financial transactions, and exposure to harassment whenever a document is presented.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no source stating whether Guerrero has enacted its own administrative procedure for legal gender recognition or whether it is among the six legislatures with nothing on the books. Guerrero's status under the March 2025 count is therefore unresolved here, and the summary states the national rule conditionally rather than asserting what applies locally.

No Guerrero-specific incidents of violence against trans people, hate-crime prosecutions, or facility and restroom rules are sourced in this inventory. Whether Guerrero recognises partners or marriages of trans visitors' spouses beyond the national position, and whether its police or clinics apply the Supreme Court guidelines in practice, remain not sourced.

The state-by-state counts are as of March 2025 and may have shifted since; the impunity figure refers to all homicides in 2022 and is not disaggregated for trans victims.
